title: The life cycle of a star
examTip: Learn both life cycles in order. One is for a star about the size of the Sun. The other is for a star much more massive. Be ready to explain the balance in a main sequence star. Know that elements heavier than iron are made in a supernova.
introTips: Every star starts as a cloud of gas and dust (nebula) pulled together by gravity.
A main sequence star is stable. Gravity pulling in is balanced by fusion energy pushing out.
The size of the star decides how its life cycle ends.
intro: Stars are born, shine for a long time, and then die. How a star ends depends on its size. In this lesson you learn how a star forms and why it stays stable. You learn the two life cycles you need. You also learn how stars make the elements.

keyPoints.heading: How a star forms and stays stable
keyPoints.content: A star forms from a cloud of dust and gas called a nebula. The Sun formed this way. Gravitational attraction pulls the dust and gas together. This makes a protostar. As more material is pulled in, the protostar gets hotter and denser. In time, it is hot and dense enough for fusion reactions to start. In fusion, light nuclei join to form heavier nuclei. Energy is released. The star is now a main sequence star. It is stable for a long time, because two effects balance. - Gravity pulls the star inwards. This is gravitational collapse. - Energy from fusion makes the star push outwards. This is expansion due to fusion energy. These two effects are in equilibrium, so the star stays the same size.
writeBullets: Star forms from a cloud of dust and gas (nebula)
Gravitational attraction pulls the dust and gas together → protostar
Protostar gets hotter and denser until fusion reactions start
Main sequence star: gravitational collapse (in) balanced by expansion due to fusion energy (out)
The balance is an equilibrium, so the star is stable

keyTerms.def: A cloud of dust and gas from which a star forms
The early stage of a star, as dust and gas are pulled together by gravity, before fusion starts
A stable star in which gravitational collapse is balanced by expansion due to fusion energy

keyPoints.memTip: Gravity squeezes in, fusion pushes out. Balanced = main sequence.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Ask the student to name the two effects that balance. Many name only gravity.

keyPoints.heading: Stars about the size of the Sun
keyPoints.content: A star goes through a life cycle. The life cycle is decided by the size of the star. A star about the same size as the Sun goes through these stages: - Nebula: a cloud of gas and dust. - Protostar. - Main sequence star: stable for most of its life. - Red giant: the star swells up when it starts to run out of fuel for fusion. - White dwarf: the star shrinks to a small, hot core. - Black dwarf: the white dwarf cools until it no longer gives out much energy.
writeBullets: The life cycle of a star is decided by its size
Sun-sized star: nebula → protostar → main sequence star
→ red giant → white dwarf → black dwarf

keyTerms.def: The stage after the main sequence for a star about the size of the Sun
The small, hot core left after a red giant
A white dwarf that has cooled down; the last stage for a star about the size of the Sun

keyPoints.memTip: Sun-sized: Red giant → White dwarf → Black dwarf. 'Really Weird Bananas'.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Ask the student to say the stages in order from the nebula. Then ask which stage the Sun is in now: main sequence.

keyPoints.heading: Stars much more massive than the Sun
keyPoints.content: A star much more massive than the Sun starts the same way. It goes from nebula to protostar to main sequence star. After that, its stages are different: - Red super giant: the star swells up to a huge size. - Supernova: the star explodes. - What is left becomes either a neutron star or a black hole.
writeBullets: Massive star: nebula → protostar → main sequence star

keyTerms.def: The stage after the main sequence for a star much more massive than the Sun
The explosion of a massive star
One possible remains of a supernova
The other possible remains of a supernova

keyPoints.memTip: Massive: Red super giant → Supernova → Neutron star or Black hole.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Students often mix the two paths. Ask: which path has the explosion? Only the massive star has a supernova.

keyPoints.heading: How stars make the elements
keyPoints.content: Fusion processes in stars produce all of the naturally occurring elements. In fusion, light nuclei join to form heavier nuclei. So lighter elements are turned into heavier elements. This is how new elements form. Fusion in a star makes elements up to iron. Elements heavier than iron are produced in a supernova. The explosion of a massive star (supernova) distributes the elements throughout the universe.
writeBullets: Fusion processes in stars produce all naturally occurring elements
Fusion joins light nuclei to make heavier nuclei, so new elements form
Elements heavier than iron are produced in a supernova
A supernova distributes the elements throughout the universe

keyTerms.def: The joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy

keyPoints.memTip: Up to iron: made in the star. Heavier than iron: made in a supernova.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Ask where the elements heavier than iron come from. The answer is a supernova, which also spreads them out.

0.question: Why does a main sequence star stay stable?
options: It has run out of fuel
Gravitational collapse is balanced by expansion due to fusion energy
Gravity has stopped acting on it
0.correctFeedback: Correct. Gravity pulls inwards and fusion energy pushes outwards. These are in equilibrium, so the star is stable.
0.wrongFeedback: In a main sequence star, gravitational collapse is balanced by expansion due to fusion energy. This equilibrium keeps the star stable.

1.question: What comes after the red giant stage for a star about the size of the Sun?
1.correctFeedback: Correct. Red giant → white dwarf → black dwarf.
1.wrongFeedback: For a Sun-sized star, the red giant becomes a white dwarf. The white dwarf then cools to a black dwarf.

2.question: A star much more massive than the Sun explodes. What is this explosion called?
2.correctFeedback: Correct. The explosion is a supernova. It leaves a neutron star or a black hole.
2.wrongFeedback: The explosion of a massive star is a supernova. It comes after the red super giant stage.

3.question: Where are elements heavier than iron produced?
options: In a main sequence star like the Sun
3.correctFeedback: Correct. Elements heavier than iron are produced in a supernova. The explosion spreads them through the universe.
3.wrongFeedback: Fusion in stars makes elements up to iron. Elements heavier than iron are produced in a supernova.

commonMistakes: Saying the Sun will end as a supernova. A star about the size of the Sun becomes a red giant, then a white dwarf.
Mixing up red giant and red super giant. Red giant is for Sun-sized stars. Red super giant is for much more massive stars.
Naming only gravity for the main sequence. Gravity is balanced by expansion due to fusion energy.
Saying all elements are made in a supernova. Only elements heavier than iron are.
examTips: Learn both life cycles as two lists in order. Say which stages they share.
For a main sequence star, name both effects that balance: gravitational collapse and expansion due to fusion energy.
When asked how elements form, mention fusion and say where elements heavier than iron are made.

Protostar → fusion starts → main sequence star
Main sequence: gravitational collapse balanced by expansion due to fusion energy
Sun-sized: main sequence → red giant → white dwarf → black dwarf
Massive: main sequence → red super giant → supernova → neutron star or black hole
Fusion in stars produces all naturally occurring elements
Elements heavier than iron are produced in a supernova
A supernova distributes the elements throughout the universe
